To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dual context (i.e., the two primes) of puns did not facilitate homonyms in comparison to single primes, but homonyms elicited a more positive N400 in the pun condition than in the neutral context condition.

The N400 elicited in a neutral context condition by the homonym tooth (i.e., a toothache or toothbrush) is more negative than the N400 eliciting in a pun context by the homonym crown (i.e., the crown of a tooth or the crown on a prince’s head).

homonyms in pun conditions elicit an N400 that is less negative than in neutral conditions, and that this N400 priming effect is not greater for puns than for single dominant biasing or subordinate biasing conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the N400 as an index of semantic featural processing, and with the N400 as a tool for understanding the processing of lexical ambiguity.
how the N400 reflects homonym processing in the unique context in which homonyms are used to make a joke.
how the human brain accesses the meaning of a homonym, and how this process is influenced by the context in which it occurs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

homonyms in pun contexts elicit a smaller N400 than homonyms in single dominant or subordinate biasing contexts, but that the N400 elicitation by puns is not enhanced in comparison to neutral homonyms.
the N400 priming effect for homonyms in a pun is not better than the N400 primings for homonyms in either dominant biasing or subordinate biasing conditions.
the N400 is a reflection of the consistency of the semantic featural information available to the brain, even in cases of dual context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
homonyms in pun contexts elicit a less consistent N400 than homonyms in single dominant biasing or subordinate biasing contexts.

the N400 amplitude is sensitive to the consistency with which various sources of semantic features converge on one lexical entry, and that this consistency is affected by the number of lexical entries that need to be accessed for the comprehension of a word.
the N400 is not a simple index of lexical-semantic activation but rather reflects the degree to which a word is consistently activated in the context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the case of homonyms in pun comprehension, two primes are not better (i.e., more facilitatory) than one.
the N400 can reflect the degree to which a word's meaning is consistent with its context.
the dual meaning of the homonym in puns is not processed more easily than the single meaning of the homophone in a neutral context.
